claim: In a UK government-commissioned survey, 37% of music creators earned GBP 5,000 or less from music in 2019, 47% earned under GBP 10,000, 62% earned GBP 20,000 or less and only 9% earned over GBP 50,000.
stance_target: The large majority of professional creative-content workers earn below a living wage from their creative work
scope_conditions: n=708 UK-resident music creators surveyed by AudienceNet for the UK Intellectual Property Office; self-reported gross income for 2019 (chosen to exclude Covid effects); not inflation-adjusted; authors state major-label artists are over-represented in the sample, which biases earnings UPWARD
quoted_support: More than a third (37%) earned £5,000 or less from music in 2019 and nearly half (47%) earned less than £10,000. 62% earned £20,000 or less from music in 2019. 9% reported earning more than £50,000 in 2019.
region: United Kingdom - WESTERN ONLY, do not generalise to Southeast Asia

claim: Among UK music creators for whom music was their only source of income, 43% earned GBP 20,000 or less and 64% earned GBP 30,000 or less in 2019, placing many full-time creators at or below the national minimum wage.
stance_target: Full-time creative work frequently pays below the statutory minimum wage
scope_conditions: n=197 respondents whose only income was music; the authors note they cannot assume all worked a full 2,080-hour year, so the minimum-wage comparison is indicative
quoted_support: The national minimum wage in 2019 (for workers over 25) was £8.21. Assuming a ‘normal’ working year of 2080 hours ... this equates to an annual salary of £17,076 ... this nonetheless suggests many musicians who gain all their earnings from music were working at around or below the minimum wage.

claim: 43% of surveyed UK music creators said that insufficient income from streaming caused them to take a job outside of music - a directly measured reason for exiting creative work.
stance_target: Inadequate income is a documented, quantified cause of creators leaving the occupation
scope_conditions: Ivors Academy / Musicians' Union poll, n=311 members of organisations actively campaigning for changes to streaming remuneration - a self-selected, motivated sample that will overstate dissatisfaction; cited secondhand in the IPO report
quoted_support: 43% said that insufficient income from streaming caused them to get a job outside of music
numbers: 92% said streaming was under 5% of earnings
50% said recorded-music income declined over 10 years

claim: Sustained streaming success is concentrated in a fraction of a percent of artists: the top 0.1% of tracks took over 40% of all UK streams every year from 2014 to 2020, the top 1% took 75-80%, and the top 10% took 95-97%.
stance_target: Attention and therefore income in creative platforms is concentrated in the extreme top tail
scope_conditions: Based on a sample of UK streaming data for each October, 2014 to 2020; track-level and artist-level figures differ and the executive summary's two 'top 1% of artists' figures (63-65% and 78-80%) appear internally inconsistent - verify against Chapter 6 before citing the artist-level numbers
quoted_support: the top 0.1% most popular tracks achieved more than 40 per cent of all streams in all years and the top 0.4 per cent of tracks accounted for more than 65% of all streams from 2016 onwards. The top 1 per cent of tracks account for between 75 and 80% and the top 10 per cent for between 95 and 97%, in all years from 2016 to 2020.

claim: Roughly 720 UK-based artists reached the streaming level the report identifies as a minimum threshold for a sustainable living in 2020, against an ONS count of 45,000 UK musicians - about 1.6%.
stance_target: The share of creators who can actually live on platform income is on the order of one to two percent
scope_conditions: The one-million-UK-streams-per-month threshold is the authors' own estimate and assumes UK streams are complemented by non-UK streams and other revenue; for solo performers and songwriters with other revenue the threshold would be lower; the 720 figure is an estimate derived from 1,723 observed artists in a single month
quoted_support: a sustained achievement of around one million UK streams per month may be some kind of guide to a minimum threshold for making a sustainable living out of music ... The number of artists achieving one million UK streams or more in October 2020 was 1723. We estimate that this 1723 UK figure may translate into around 720 UK artists achieving this level of success in 2020
numbers: 1,723 artists reached 1 million UK streams in October 2020

claim: Streaming royalties account for only 6% of the average UK music creator's income while live performance accounts for 31%, so the headline digital revenue channel is a minor part of actual creator earnings.
stance_target: Platform-native revenue is a small share of what creators actually live on
scope_conditions: n=637 respondents who earned money from music in 2019; pre-pandemic shares; averages across respondents, not shares of total industry revenue
quoted_support: Prior to the Covid-19 pandemic, live performances were by far the single greatest source of income on average, generating nearly one third (31%) of respondents' music related income. No other source, including individual ‘other’ sources, accounted for more than 9% of music related income. Audio streaming royalties accounted, on average, for 6% of income

claim: Median UK music income in 2019 varied more than fourfold by contractual status, from GBP 51,816 for artists signed to major labels down to GBP 12,944 for self-releasing artists.
stance_target: Institutional backing rather than independent effort determines creator earnings
scope_conditions: Self-reported 2019 income within the n=708 survey; only 38 of 477 performers were signed to majors so that median rests on a small cell; the authors note major-label artists are over-represented relative to the UK musician population
quoted_support: Median reported income for those currently signed to major record companies (£51,816 in 2019) is considerably higher than for all other groups of artists, with those previously signed to major record companies next (£25,500). Median reported income for those signed to independent record companies is £20,250 and for self-releasing artists it is £12,944

claim: Female music creators reported a median 2019 income of GBP 13,057 against GBP 20,160 for men, a gap of 35%.
stance_target: Creator earnings gaps track demographic lines as well as audience size
scope_conditions: Self-reported within the n=708 survey; women are under-represented in the sample, which the authors accept as matching the population of musicians
quoted_support: Median reported income for women in 2019 was £13,057, whereas for men it was £20,160

claim: Record labels historically churned 30-50% of their signed artists every year, establishing that high attrition in creative careers long predates digital platforms.
stance_target: Platform algorithms are the cause of high creator attrition
scope_conditions: Monopolies and Mergers Commission 1994 inquiry into UK record companies, cited secondhand; refers to major-label rosters in the late 1980s and early 1990s, a pre-digital population of a few hundred artists
quoted_support: Typically the majors gained and dropped between 30 and 50 per cent of their artists each year’. PolyGram, one of the then five major record companies of the time, ‘had some 445 different artists under contract between 1989 and 1992 but fewer than half that number at any one time
numbers: fewer than half under contract at any one time
only 15 artists remained contracted to one major's pop labels 1 Jan 1988 to 30 June 1993
at least 20 UK artists a year released a first 100,000-selling album from 1985

claim: More than 90% of performers across 27 European countries receive under EUR 1,000 per year from streaming, according to a survey of over 5,800 performers.
stance_target: Sub-subsistence platform earnings are a Europe-wide pattern, not a UK artefact
scope_conditions: #PayPerformers survey commissioned by European collective management organisations, which are advocating for higher performer remuneration - an advocacy-commissioned survey with an interest in low reported figures; cited secondhand in the IPO report
quoted_support: The survey of over 5800 performers across 27 European countries commissioned by European CMOs finds more than 90% of performers receive less than €1000 per year from streaming.
region: 27 European countries - WESTERN, does not generalise to Southeast Asia

claim: The proportion of UK music creators earning nothing at all from music doubled from 4% in 2019 to 8% in 2020, while the share earning over GBP 50,000 barely moved, showing shocks fall on the bottom of the distribution.
stance_target: Income shocks in creative work are absorbed almost entirely by low and mid-tier creators
scope_conditions: n=708; 2020 is the first pandemic year so the shock is Covid-specific, though the distributional asymmetry is the finding of interest
quoted_support: The proportion of musicians earning nothing from music doubled between 2019 and the first pandemic year of 2020, from 4% to 8%.

claim: A typical songwriter earns about GBP 1,176 from one million streams in a four-week month, annualising to GBP 15,288, which is below the UK median full-time salary of GBP 31,461.
stance_target: Even hitting an aspirational streaming milestone does not produce a median wage
scope_conditions: The report's own modelled estimate, corrected in the published errata to account for a 5% PRS/ICE administration fee; assumes the same stream level sustained across a year; based on 2020 rates
quoted_support: the true figure for a month (=four weeks) should therefore be £1,176 (£11,000 x 15% publishing rights share (= £1,650) – 5% PRS/ICE fee (= £1567.50) x 75% average typical songwriter rate = £1,176). On this basis, the annual figure if the same level of streams were sustained across a year would be £15,288.
numbers: featured performer GBP 1,201 per million streams
